html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Assess readiness and prepare the release, including the model card and conformity
  • Monitor continuously and keep a schedule for maintenance, updates and retraining
  • Run periodic assessments: security tests, audits, red teaming and threat modeling
  • Handle and record incidents, issues and risks
  • Work with stakeholders to find why incidents happen
  • Make the disclosures that transparency duties require

2III.C.1: Judge readiness and prepare the release

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Assess, so the depth is Evaluate. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Running case

Release, a Wrong Refund and a Shift in Applicants

  • The hiring tool is ready for a gate review; Daniel Osei brings the model card and the conformity evidence
  • Weeks after launch, the assistant tells a customer about a refund window that does not exist; the cause is out-of-date support documents
  • After a hiring campaign in a new region, monitoring flags a shift in the input data
  • Mei Tanaka's team plans a red-team test; Lucia Moreno asks what Helios must disclose to candidates

Release Readiness: The Gate and the Checklist

  • A release gate decides whether the system is ready for production
  • Tests passed against the thresholds set earlier; residual risks accepted by the owner
  • Documentation complete: model card, instructions for use, technical documentation
  • Conformity requirements satisfied where a law requires them
  • Operations ready: a monitoring plan, a rollback or shutdown plan, support and training, and a communication plan
  • No gate, no go-live: missing items are conditions, not afterthoughts

Exam tip

Readiness is wider than test results: it includes documents, approvals and the ability to monitor and roll back.

The Release Package: Model Card, Instructions and Records

  • Model card (module 9): intended use, performance by group, evaluation conditions, limitations
  • Instructions for use for deployers: provider identity, capabilities and limits, oversight measures, resources and lifetime, log collection (Article 13)
  • Technical documentation (Article 11, Annex IV) and the risk assessment record
  • Test and validation reports, approvals and version identifiers
  • Monitoring plan and incident contacts
  • Helios: Daniel Osei assembles the package for the committee's launch gate
Exam tip

The deployer can only oversee what the provider tells it, so the instructions for use are part of the release, not an extra.

Satisfying Conformity Requirements

  • EU high-risk systems: conformity assessment (Article 43), EU declaration (Article 47), CE marking (Article 48) and registration (Article 49) before placing on the market
  • A substantial modification after release needs a new assessment; changes pre-determined for a learning system are not substantial
  • Elsewhere: sector rules, state laws and contract commitments may add checks (for example audits of hiring tools)
  • Standards such as ISO/IEC 42001 can help organize the evidence
  • The release gate tracks each requirement with an owner

Exam tip

Conformity comes before market placement, not after the first problem.

Staged Release and Rollback

  • Staged release: start with a small share of users, then widen as monitoring stays healthy
  • Feature flags and canaries: turn parts on or off, and compare against the old version
  • Rollback criteria: the thresholds that trigger a return to the previous version or a pause
  • Kill switch: a tested way to stop the system (NIST: mechanisms to supersede, disengage or deactivate)
  • Support readiness: staff know how to escalate, and users know how to reach a person
  • Helios: the hiring tool starts with one region and an agreed rollback trigger
Exam tip

A rollback that has never been tested is not a rollback plan.

3III.C.2: Monitor continuously and schedule maintenance, updates and retraining

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Conduct, so the depth is Apply. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

What to Monitor

  • Performance: accuracy and error rates against the thresholds
  • Data and drift: changes in inputs and outputs over time
  • Fairness: outcomes by group, compared with launch
  • Safety and security: abuse, attacks and harmful outputs
  • Usage and feedback: volume, complaints, appeals and human overrides
  • Operations: latency, availability and cost
  • NIST asks for approaches to track existing, unanticipated and emergent risks (MEASURE 3.1)

Exam tip

Monitor what can go wrong for people, not only what can go wrong for the server.

Drift: Data, Concept and Model

  • Data drift: the mix of inputs changes (Helios: applicants from a new region)
  • Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and the right answer changes (a new refund policy)
  • Performance drift: accuracy or fairness falls; it may lag the other two
  • Detect: compare input distributions and outputs with the training baseline; track metrics by group
  • React: investigate, retrain or recalibrate, or roll back, then retest
  • NIST notes that systems may need more frequent maintenance because of data, model or concept drift

Exam tip

Data drift can appear before accuracy drops; that early warning is why you monitor inputs.

Maintenance, Updates and Retraining

  • A maintenance schedule sets regular reviews, security patches, dependency updates and data refreshes
  • Scheduled retraining keeps the model current; triggered retraining responds to drift, incidents, new data or a new law
  • Every change goes through change control: test, approve, release in stages, monitor
  • A substantial modification may need new conformity assessment (module 6)
  • Document each version: data, settings, results, approver
  • Retire the model when it cannot be kept safe or useful

Exam tip

Retraining is a change like any other: it needs testing and approval before it goes live.

Monitoring in Practice: Owners, Thresholds, Alerts, Logs

  • Owners: each metric has a named owner and a review rhythm
  • Thresholds and alerts: warning and action levels, with who is paged
  • Logs: the system records events for traceability (AI Act Article 12), and logs are kept for the period the rules require
  • Human review of samples: people read a sample of real outputs, because metrics miss some failures
  • Escalation: alerts above the action level go to the incident process
  • Post-market monitoring plan: the provider's documented system for collecting performance data over the system's life (Article 72)
Exam tip

Monitoring without owners, thresholds and an escalation path is just data collection.

4III.C.3: Run periodic checks of performance, reliability and safety

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Conduct, so the depth is Apply. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Periodic Assessment: What, How Often, Who

  • Continuous monitoring watches the live system; periodic assessments step back and test it harder
  • Audits: compliance with policy and law
  • Red teaming: trying to make the system fail or misbehave
  • Threat modeling: how an attacker could reach and abuse it
  • Security testing: vulnerabilities in code, models and infrastructure
  • Set frequency by risk, and also run them after major changes

Exam tip

Match the assessment to the question: policy compliance is an audit, breaking the system is red teaming, mapping attack paths is threat modeling.

Audits of AI Systems

  • Internal audit: the third line checks governance and risk management (module 2)
  • External or independent audit: an outside party examines compliance and controls; ISO/IEC 42001 certification relies on audits of the management system
  • Scope: policy compliance, data and model records, testing evidence, monitoring, incident handling
  • Evidence: documents, logs, test results and interviews
  • Outputs: findings, owners and due dates; follow-up audits confirm fixes
  • Bias audits: some laws, such as New York City's rule for hiring tools, require independent bias audits (module 6)
Exam tip

An audit looks backward at evidence; it does not replace testing the system's behavior.

Red Teaming

  • Red teaming is a structured attempt to make the system fail or misbehave, as a determined misuser would
  • Methods: misuse and jailbreak attempts, bias probes, data-extraction attempts, harmful-output tests
  • Independent testers see what builders miss; mix internal and external skills
  • Findings are rated, fixed and retested
  • The AI Act requires adversarial testing for general-purpose models with systemic risk (Article 55)
  • Helios: Mei Tanaka's team tests the assistant for abuse and data leakage

Exam tip

Red teaming tests what an adversary could make the system do; it is broader than normal acceptance testing.

Threat Modeling and AI-Specific Attacks Beyond the BoK

  • Threat modeling: list assets, attackers, entry points and abuse cases, then plan controls
  • Data poisoning: tampering with training data
  • Evasion: inputs crafted to cause mistakes
  • Model extraction: copying a model by querying it
  • Inversion and membership inference: recovering or detecting training data
  • Prompt injection: hidden instructions in input that hijack a language model
  • Reference lists exist: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems: adversary tactics against AI) and the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10 for LLM Applications

Exam tip

You need to recognize each attack by its description, not to know how to carry it out.

Security Testing, Reliability and Safety Checks

  • Security testing: penetration tests of the application and APIs, vulnerability scans, tests for leakage and access control
  • Model-level tests: adversarial inputs, poisoning checks, extraction and inversion attempts, prompt-injection tests
  • Reliability checks: performance under stress, noise and drift, failover and recovery
  • Safety checks: do outputs or actions harm people in foreseeable use or misuse?
  • Supply chain: check third-party models, data and components (module 3)
  • Record results, fix findings, and feed them back into the risk register
Exam tip

Security, reliability and safety are three different questions; one passing test does not answer the others.

5III.C.4: Handle incidents, issues and risks and keep records of them

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Manage, so the depth is Apply. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

What Counts as an AI Incident

  • An incident is an event in which an AI system causes or could cause harm, or fails or behaves unexpectedly
  • Examples: a wrong or harmful output, a biased outcome pattern, a data leak, a security breach, a safety event, an outage that affects people
  • Near misses matter: log them and learn
  • An issue is a smaller problem to fix; a risk is something that may happen; keep separate registers, linked
  • Severity depends on harm to people, legal duties and scale
  • Helios: the assistant's wrong refund answer is an incident, and a pattern of them would be a bigger one
Exam tip

A near miss is cheap information: record it.

The Incident Response Cycle

  • Detect and report: monitoring, users, staff or a partner raises it
  • Triage: set severity and the owner
  • Contain: pause, limit or correct the system to stop further harm
  • Investigate: find the root cause
  • Remediate and retest, then communicate to those affected and to authorities where required
  • Learn: update tests, thresholds and documents; document at every step

Exam tip

Contain before you investigate: stop the harm first, then find the cause.

Reporting Clocks and Records

Source Clock
EU AI Act, serious incident (provider, Article 73) not later than 15 days after awareness; 2 days for a widespread infringement; 10 days after a death
GDPR personal data breach (controller, Article 33) not later than 72 hours after awareness, where feasible
Contracts customer and vendor agreements may set shorter notice
Internal policy escalation to the committee, as set by the AI policy
  • Communicate incidents to affected people and relevant parties, with plain information (NIST MANAGE 4.3)
  • Keep the incident record: facts, effects, actions and the lessons learned
Exam tip

One incident can start several clocks at once; the shortest applicable limit governs.

Issue and Risk Registers, and Learning

  • Risk register: risks, likelihood and severity, controls, owners, status; updated after each incident
  • Issue log: problems found in operation, with severity, owner, due date and closure evidence
  • Incident register: every incident and near miss, with root cause and corrective actions
  • Trends: repeated issues point to a systemic cause; report them to the committee
  • Lessons learned: change tests, thresholds, training and documents, and record what changed
  • Post-deployment plans should include appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery and change management (NIST MANAGE 4.1)
Exam tip

An incident that does not change a control, a test or a document has not been learned from.

6III.C.5: Work with stakeholders to find why incidents arise

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Collaborate, so the depth is Apply. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Why AI Incidents Arise: Five Causes

  • Brittleness: the system works only in narrow conditions and breaks outside them
  • Weak robustness: it fails under noise, odd inputs or attack
  • Poor data: stale, wrong or unrepresentative data (the Helios refund error)
  • Insufficient testing: a case or change that was never tested
  • Drift: the data or the world changed since training
  • Often several causes combine

Exam tip

Name the cause from the symptom: stale answers point to data, sudden failure on new inputs to brittleness, slow decay to drift.

Root-Cause Analysis With Cross-Functional Teams

  • Why cross-functional: causes cross boundaries: data, model, process, content and use
  • Who: data science, engineering, the business owner, content owners, legal and privacy, security, and support
  • Methods: a timeline of events, five whys, a cause-and-effect diagram
  • Blameless review: find system causes, not culprits
  • Output: causes, corrective actions, owners and dates
  • Helios: support content owners join data science to trace the refund error

Exam tip

A purely technical review misses process and content causes; bring the people who own each link in the chain.

Helios: Two Incidents, Two Root Causes

Incident Likely cause Corrective action
Wrong refund window from the assistant out-of-date support documents in the retrieval source (poor data, weak change control) refresh and version the documents, add an owner and review date, test answers against policy changes
Shift in input data after a new-region campaign data drift: the applicant mix changed re-test fairness and performance on the new mix, retrain or recalibrate, add drift alerts
  • Common thread: the data changed and nobody owned the change
  • Both feed the risk register and the test plan
Exam tip

Fix the process that let the cause through, not only the single wrong answer.

From Cause to Prevention

  • Poor data: data owners, freshness rules, quality checks at the source, change control
  • Insufficient testing: regression tests for every incident, test sets that include edge cases and policy changes
  • Brittleness and weak robustness: stress and adversarial testing, input validation, fallbacks to a person
  • Drift: monitoring with alerts, scheduled and triggered retraining
  • Governance: update the risk register, thresholds and instructions after each incident
  • Share lessons with the deployers and, where required, authorities
Exam tip

Every cause needs a matching control, and every incident should add a test.

7III.C.6: Make the public disclosures that transparency duties require

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Make, so the depth is Apply. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Public Disclosures: What, to Whom

  • Authorities and assessors: technical documentation and logs on request
  • Deployers: instructions for use, capabilities and limits, oversight measures (Article 13)
  • People affected and users: notices that AI is used, and where required, explanations (Article 50 and modules 4 and 6)
  • The public: registration entries and summaries where the law requires them
  • Helios: tells candidates that AI screens applications and how to ask for a person

Exam tip

Disclosure follows the audience: authorities get documentation, deployers get instructions, people get notices.

Instructions for Use and Technical Documentation

  • Instructions for use must be clear and accessible to deployers: provider identity, capabilities and limitations, pre-determined changes, human oversight measures, resources and lifetime, log collection (Article 13)
  • Technical documentation (Article 11, Annex IV) is kept current and supplied to authorities on request
  • Accuracy levels and metrics are declared in the instructions (Article 15)
  • Update both when the system changes
  • Deployers use the instructions to meet their own duties, so gaps pass downstream
Exam tip

If the instructions for use are vague, the deployer cannot oversee the system properly.

Post-Market Plans, Registration and Public Summaries [Verify live]

  • Post-market monitoring plan: part of the technical documentation (Article 72); it shows how the provider will watch the system after release
  • EU database: information registered for high-risk systems under Article 49 is publicly accessible in a user-friendly form, except one protected section (Article 71)
  • General-purpose models: publish the training-content summary (module 6)
  • Hiring tools in New York City: a public summary of the independent bias audit
  • As of 27 October 2026: disclosure rules differ by jurisdiction and are still developing; confirm each duty at release
Exam tip

Public disclosure is limited and specific: registration entries, notices and summaries, not the whole technical file.

8Exam Q&A

8.1 Practice questions (one best answer, or select exactly the number the question asks for)

S1Helios's hiring tool passes all its tests, but its model card is incomplete and no monitoring plan exists. What should the release gate decide?

  • ARelease now and finish the model card and monitoring plan within the first month of use
  • BHold the release until the model card and monitoring plan are done, since readiness covers both
  • CRelease to the regions together, because passing the tests shows that the system is safe
  • DSkip the monitoring plan, because monitoring is the deployer's task and is not part of release readiness
Show the answer

Answer: B. Readiness covers tests, documentation, approvals, monitoring and rollback together. A system that cannot be monitored or explained is not ready, whatever the test results.

S2Which TWO items belong in the release readiness review of a high-risk EU system? (Select TWO.)

  • AThe date and guest list for the public launch event and the press release for the product
  • BThe size of the sales commission that will be paid on the first customer contracts
  • CEvidence that the conformity assessment, declaration, marking and registration are complete
  • DThe color scheme and logo that will appear on the system's user interface screens
  • EA tested rollback or shutdown plan and a monitoring plan with named owners and thresholds
Show the answer

Answer: C, E. A release review checks conformity evidence and operational readiness, including a tested rollback and a monitoring plan with owners and thresholds. Event planning, commissions and visual design are not readiness criteria.

S3A deployed model's input data start to differ from its training data, but accuracy has not yet fallen. What is happening, and what should the team do?

  • ANothing is wrong, because accuracy is the only measure that matters for a deployed model
  • BThis is a security attack, so the team should shut the system down and delete the logs
  • CThis is a hardware fault, so the team should replace the servers and leave the model unchanged
  • DThis is data drift, so the team should investigate and decide on retraining or recalibration
Show the answer

Answer: D. A change in the input mix is data drift, an early warning that can precede a fall in accuracy. The team investigates and retrains or recalibrates if needed, then retests.

S4Which approach best fits a model whose data change quickly?

  • AScheduled reviews and threshold-triggered retraining, with testing and approval before redeployment
  • BRetraining once at launch and not again, because the model has already been tested in production
  • CRetraining nightly and deploying the new version straight away, with no testing or approval step
  • DWaiting for customers to complain before the model is reviewed, retrained or rolled back to its earlier state
Show the answer

Answer: A. A schedule keeps the model current, triggers respond to drift and incidents, and change control tests and approves each new version. Never retraining, untested automatic deployment and waiting for complaints are all weak.

S5Which TWO activities are periodic assessments of an AI system's performance, reliability and safety? (Select TWO.)

  • AWriting the advertising copy that describes the system to prospective customers and the press
  • BA structured red-team exercise that tries to make the system fail or misbehave
  • CChoosing the font used in the system's documentation and the layout of the help pages
  • DAn independent audit of the system's controls, testing evidence and monitoring records
  • ECounting how many staff attended the company's annual holiday celebration this year
Show the answer

Answer: B, D. Red teaming and independent audits are periodic assessments of performance, reliability, safety and controls, alongside threat modeling and security testing. The other activities have nothing to do with assessing the system.

S6The Helios assistant tells a customer about a refund window that does not exist. What is the best response sequence?

  • AWait for further complaints, and then decide whether the matter is serious enough to be examined
  • BChange the model's name and release it again, so that earlier complaints no longer refer to the same system
  • CContain the harm, log the incident, find the root cause, fix and retest, and communicate as required
  • DDelete the conversation logs, so that the wrong answer is hard to trace back to the company or its staff
Show the answer

Answer: C. Incident handling means containing the harm, recording the incident, finding the root cause, fixing and retesting, and communicating as required. Waiting, renaming or deleting evidence makes the problem worse.

S7After a hiring campaign in a new region, the applicant mix changes and a model's results shift. Which cause of AI incidents does this best illustrate?

  • AInsufficient testing of the user interface, because the buttons were placed in the wrong order
  • BData drift, because the inputs the model now sees differ from those it was trained on
  • CA weak password policy, because employees reused credentials across several internal systems
  • DBrittleness caused by a hardware failure in the data center that hosts the model
Show the answer

Answer: B. A changed input mix is data drift: the model now sees data unlike its training data. Interface layout, passwords and hardware are not the cause.

S8Who should take part in the root-cause review of the wrong refund answer?

  • AOnly the data scientists, since the model produced the answer and nobody else touches the system
  • BThe lawyers, because refunds are a legal matter and technical staff would slow the review down
  • CThe customer who received the answer, because that person is the one who was affected by it
  • DA cross-functional group: data science, engineering, content owners, legal, privacy and security
Show the answer

Answer: D. The causes cross data, model, content, process and legal duties, so the review needs the people who own each link in the chain, not a single function.

S9Which of these is made publicly available for a high-risk system under the EU AI Act?

  • ARegistration information entered in the EU database, apart from one protected section
  • BThe provider's complete technical documentation, including its source code and training data
  • CThe system's internal risk register and the logs of its individual decisions
  • DThe unpublished test reports that the provider keeps for its own internal quality control
Show the answer

Answer: A. Information registered in the EU database is publicly accessible in a user-friendly form, with one protected section. Technical documentation and logs go to authorities on request, and internal registers and test reports are not published.
